title: Paul's Divine Calling and God's Sovereign Order in Salvation
english: Paul, chosen for the gospel of God, affirms in his letter to the Galatians that when God found it pleasing, He set him apart from his mother’s womb to reveal His Son within him. Those who misunderstand God’s foreknowledge and predestination twist these words, supposing they point only to those preserved by nature and constitution, while others even deny what rests within our power, citing the psalm that declares sinners alienated from the womb. Yet this is readily answered by examining the words that follow: it is written that sinners are estranged from the womb, they have strayed from birth, they have uttered lies; their fury bears the likeness of the serpent. We must challenge those who take these words literally: if those sinners, alienated from the womb, had immediately wandered from the path of salvation and spoken falsehood upon birth by their own accord, how could they have done so? For they could not have formed a coherent infant voice to speak lies at the moment of delivery. But if we reflect on what was said earlier in this very letter about predestination, we can, by setting aside those who mislead the simple into accusing God of injustice, uphold the truth that God both sets apart from the womb and sets apart for the gospel of God the servant Jesus Christ, known as the apostle Paul. Thus it stands: we know that for those who love God, all things work together for good, for those called according to purpose; whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He might be the firstborn among many brothers; and whom He predestined, He also called; and whom He called, He also justified; and whom He justified, He also glorified. Therefore, let us follow the sequence of what has been said: God justifies because He called beforehand; He would not justify those He did not call; and He calls because He predestined beforehand; He would not call those He did not predestine; and it is to Him that the beginning of the call and justification belongs, not predestination. For if predestination were the starting point of what follows, those who advance the strange argument of nature would easily prevail. But above predestination lies foreknowledge: for whom He foreknew, He declares, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son. God, having beforehand attended to the order of coming things, and having considered the inclination of these things in us toward security and impulse after that inclination, and as they will surrender themselves wholly to living according to virtue, He foreknew them, knowing the present and foreknowing the future; and whom He so foreknew, He predestined to be conformed as sons in the image of His Son. Therefore there is the Son of God, who is the image of the invisible God, and this is the image spoken of—the image of the Son of God—which we believe to be the soul the Son of God assumed, human, formed through the virtue of God’s image into an image. And this, which we regard as an image of an image [of the Son] of God, God has predestined to become conformed through His foreknowledge concerning them; yet we must not suppose that God’s foreknowledge is the cause of future things. Rather, since He was about to act according to His own impulse, He foreknew, knowing all things before their generation; and as knowing all things before their generation, He foreknew and predestined some to be conformed as sons in the image of His Son, and saw others as alienated.

We must not confuse the order of divine action: it is not that God first predestines and then calls, but that His foreknowledge precedes and undergirds both. The psalm’s words about sinners alienated from the womb are not to be read as a denial of human responsibility, but as a description of a condition that, from birth, inclines toward falsehood—yet even then, the capacity for choice remains, however dim. To imagine that infants could speak lies in unison at birth is to misunderstand both language and moral agency. But when we read Paul’s own words in Galatians, we see that his separation from the womb was not a mere natural endowment, but a divine act aimed at revealing Christ in him—thus grounding the apostolic calling in God’s purpose, not human merit. This is why we affirm that all things work together for good for those who love God, not because they earned it, but because they were called according to His eternal purpose. The chain is clear: foreknowledge leads to predestination, predestination to calling, calling to justification, justification to glorification—each step dependent on the prior, none originating in predestination alone. If we reverse this order and make predestination the first cause, we open the door to those who would blame God for injustice, as if He arbitrarily chose some and rejected others. But Scripture refuses such a reading: God’s foreknowledge is not the cause of what comes to be, but the reflection of His knowledge of what will be, grounded in His eternal understanding of hearts inclined toward virtue or alienation. Thus, He foreknew some as those who would yield to virtue, others as those who would remain alienated—not because He made them so, but because He saw what they would become, in freedom, before time began.

title: Divine Foreknowledge and Human Responsibility in Salvation
english: If someone insists these events could not have taken place, we respond that they might not have occurred, but it does not follow that if something is incapable of happening, it must either happen or fail to happen; events unfold not solely by necessity, but also as contingent possibilities, including the possibility of non-occurrence. The examination of what is possible engages both logical analysis and reflective insight, enabling one who turns inward to perceive the subtlety of arguments and grasp how even fortuitous occurrences do not obstruct the potential for something to be actual in multiple ways—one of many possibilities becoming real, not by compulsion. God foreknew that events would unfold not through necessity but as free possibilities, and the declaration that they would occur is not speculative guesswork but genuine foreknowledge. Let no one suppose we have remained silent on predestination as if it were a heavy burden, for Paul affirms we know that all things cooperate for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. Yet observe how the apostle immediately identifies the ground of this calling: those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be shaped into the likeness of his Son. Who, then, is more fitting for the righteous vocation grounded in God’s purpose than those who love him? Indeed, he makes clear the source of this calling lies within us—our purpose and foreknowledge: we know that all things work together for good for those who love God. For he nearly said that such cooperation occurs because those who love God are worthy partners in the good. At the same time, let us challenge those who speak contrary views and demand they answer us. Assume hypothetically that something depends on us; we will tell them they reject what depends on us until their argument collapses under the weight of the given hypothesis as unsound. Given that something depends on us, does God, by ordaining the sequence of future events, foreknow what will arise from what depends on us in each case where such dependence exists, or does he not? To claim he does not foreknow is to overlook the universal intellect and grandeur of God. But if they affirm he does foreknow, let us ask: is his foreknowledge the cause of what will come to pass, given that what depends on us exists? Or, since he foreknew, is foreknowledge entirely irrelevant as a cause of what depends on us? It was possible for some of these individuals, having answered otherwise, to have acted differently, and the self-determining creature brought into being could have chosen otherwise. In such discourses, the words 'Well done, good and faithful servant' are preserved, as well as 'You have been faithful over little; I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord.' Likewise preserved is the reasonable utterance of the wicked and slothful servant: 'You ought to have put my money to the exchangers.' Only justly spoken words will endure: to those on the right, 'Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,' because I was hungry and you gave me food, and what follows; but to those on the left, 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,' because I was hungry and you gave me no food, nor what follows. Moreover, even if one were set apart for the gospel of God from the womb and had necessity imposed upon them, how could they consistently speak of subduing their body and leading into slavery if they had not yet been declared unapproved by others, and the woe would be theirs if they did not evangelize? Clearly, from this it follows that if they had not subdued their body and led into slavery, it would have been possible for them to be declared unapproved by others, and it was possible for woe to befall them had they not evangelized. Perhaps God both set them apart from the womb and for the gospel of God, together with perceiving the cause of the just separation: that they would subdue their body and lead into slavery, wary lest they themselves, while proclaiming, become unapproved; and knowing that woe would come upon them if they did not evangelize, they did not remain silent out of fear of God regarding the woe, but evangelized. And these things were seen by the one who set them apart from their mother’s womb and the one who set them apart for their own gospel: that there would be labors, imprisonments, beatings beyond measure, frequent deaths; by the Jews five times forty lashes minus one, three times beaten with rods, once stoned; and these things will happen to them.

title: Divine Calling and Apostolic Ministry
english: Boasting in trials and recognizing that trials forge endurance, and endurance—because of this, it was proper for him to be designated for God’s gospel, foreknown to exist and to be set apart from his mother’s womb. He was appointed to the gospel of God not due to any exceptional nature, nor because of superiority over other natures, but because of previously known deeds and later actions born of preparation and apostolic choice. At present, it was not fitting to deliver what is written in the psalm, for it would be digressive; thus, in the divine ordering, it will be given when we recount the psalm—this will be sufficient, even in excess, for the one who is set apart. For God is my witness, whom I serve in spirit through the gospel of his Son, as I continually remember you in my prayers, asking that I might at last come to you by God’s will, for I long to see you. Indeed, someone may come not according to God’s will, just as Balaam went to Balak, cursing Israel for hire; I also believe that every Gentile, or whenever the worship of God is foreign, not ministering to the beneficial holy things for them, does not prosper in God’s purpose to become toward those they approach, even if they thrive temporarily—what does scripture say about the evil prosperity of man? That I may impart to you a spiritual gift to establish you; this is indeed mutual encouragement among you through the faith you share, yours and mine. Regarding a gift that is not spiritual, I consider it necessarily follows: there are non-spiritual gifts, such as marriage, for the spiritual gift can never be hindered by prayer, yet the union of man and woman impedes it. The apostle indicates marriage as a gift when he says, ‘I wish all people were as I am,’ yet each has his own gift from God—one in this manner, another in that. I do not wish you to be unaware, brothers, that I often planned to come to you and was hindered until now, so that I might bear fruit among you, just as I have among other nations—Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish—and I am a debtor, so that my eagerness and you in Rome may preach the gospel. [But here is a parenthetical remark, which, if ignored, disrupts the sequence; for who would claim Paul was hindered from coming to the Romans in order to bear fruit? On the contrary, if he had not been hindered, he would have borne fruit; but being hindered, he was deprived of it—how then should we read? Often I planned to come to you that I might bear fruit among you, just as I have among other nations, Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish, and I was hindered until now; therefore, why was the parenthetical inserted? Because the purpose clause ‘that I may bear fruit’ was about to connect with much—for example, ‘that I also bear fruit among the other nations, Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish, I am a debtor, and the following’—so that it would not break continuity. Having inserted ‘I was hindered until now,’ he joined it to the former ‘I planned to come to you’ and the ‘that I may bear fruit,’ thus restoring the discourse’s order.] For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of people who suppress the truth in injustice. It also seems to be spoken of as wrath and the servant of those who have sinned laboring, and those under him of the same servants and ministers, as when God’s wrath was set to burn in Israel, when he caused David to rise against them, he commanded Joab to number the people; but the second stands from having sent out their wrath, anger, and tribulation, vengeance through evil angels. But then, those who labor through sin—I hear according to the allotment and unrepentant heart, he stirs up anger within himself on the day of wrath, and the fact that he has reached yet his anger to the end. Regarding these matters, consider whether the things happening to the righteous, when the evil one tempts them, wrath is indeed not from God nor from heaven, but from below somewhere, or from the devil or some of his angels; yet for these, no one plausibly argues that we are to wage war before the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, for these things will appear as those who are angry tearing apart the holy ones and bringing upon them wrath from heaven. english: Just as what is lower has been revealed, so too does divine wrath from heaven rest upon us—though one might ask whether this wrath comes from heaven but not from God. If God has made truth known to all through the reasoning found in nature, and has revealed himself to each according to their capacity to complete that reasoning, then judgment must follow upon all ungodly and unjust deeds—more heavily for some, less for others—in proportion, so that the revelation of God’s heavenly wrath may be fulfilled. To those who, through steadfastness in good works, pursue glory, honor, and immortality, eternal life is given; but to those driven by rivalry, who reject truth while embracing injustice, wrath and anger, distress and anguish come upon every soul that does evil—first the Jew, then the Greek. Wrath is the punishment that follows sin; anger, they say, is wrath roused and made manifest, serving to convict when one suffers from sin—either through conscience being struck or through troubles that follow sin. Yet distress also follows such people, not from endurance itself, nor from fasting done for show, but only when it is bound up with anguish. No one would feel straitened if they had widened their heart like a snake’s girth and heard the apostle say, ‘Be widened, you also.’ For evil things tend to gather and narrow the soul, as the devil lies in ambush like a serpent. Glory, honor, and peace belong to everyone who does good—first the Jew, then the Greek—for God shows no partiality. Thus, the one who does good and valuable deeds, revealing their own worth, will receive honor by rising through repentance, from which they fell having become like senseless beasts; and having grasped what is worthy of immortality, they are raised in glory to eternal life. And in peace is everyone who is undistracted, not drawn aside by anything else to think or act against the truth, according to how God’s peace guards your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus—may peace be multiplied to you, and I give you my peace; and the prophet declares that peace will abound in the Lord’s visitation, so that false light, both by day and night, may cease to exist. For those who sinned without law will also perish without law, and those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law; for it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers who will be justified. Judgment comes according to law and through law, but destruction does not submit to law—nor does anyone else destroy them so that they may be judged by a law of destruction, but destruction holds those who sinned without law. Yet those who sinned under the law, not having utterly deserted it, whether by neglect or being overcome, yet still intending to live by it, will be judged by the law. With their conscience bearing witness and their thoughts accusing or excusing one another, on the day when God judges the secrets of humanity according to my gospel through Jesus Christ. [Or thus:] God judges according to the gospel, which is Paul’s gospel, and those who have made themselves worthy like him—among whom there is no sorrowful person, but only cause for joy—thus their gospel stands with God’s judgment as a minister entrusted with it. Therefore, the one who teaches something else about themselves, do they not teach themselves? The one who preaches against stealing, do they steal? The one who says not to commit adultery, do they commit adultery? The one who abhors idols, do they rob temples? The one who boasts in the law, yet transgresses it, do they dishonor God? For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations as it is written. Circumcision profits if you keep the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. One must inquire how often the law is spoken, especially by the apostle, so as not to appear to contradict oneself; at times when one is circumcised, Christ does not benefit you at all; at other times, circumcision helps if one practices the law. title: The Spiritual Advantage of Jews and Gentiles in Relation to the Law and Circumcision
english: When the Gentiles, who lack the written law, nevertheless fulfill its requirements by innate disposition, Paul speaks of a nature that is not merely biological but moral—a law written in the conscience. He extends the term “law” beyond the Torah of Moses to include the prophetic writings, as when he cites Isaiah: ‘In strange tongues and through foreign lips they will speak to this people.’ Even Christ’s ethical teaching, he suggests, functions as a law—not the law of Sinai, but the law of grace embodied in obedience to God through Christ. Thus, when Paul declares that those who seek justification by the law are severed from grace, he is not rejecting moral effort but overturning reliance on the external letter of Moses, which cannot impart life. Circumcision, he clarifies, is not the physical mutilation some imagine, but a spiritual reality: the cutting away of corruption from the heart. One who is inwardly circumcised by the Spirit profits not from ritual observance but from the renewal of the soul, which enables the practice of righteousness. Yet Paul also acknowledges that the law can be interpreted externally, through exposition, as when he addresses those from Judea: he became as a Jew to win Jews, having circumcised Timothy and observed ritual purity, not to compromise the gospel but to remove avoidable offense. To the Gentiles, however, he refuses to impose circumcision, not because he is inconsistent, but because the Abrahamic promise includes Gentile believers not as proselytes bound by Levitical codes, but as heirs through faith. The Levites, priests, and elders were never commanded to impose such rites on converts; God’s concern was always for the heart, not the periphery. When the sacred rites of sanctification were observed, both native Israelites and resident foreigners brought offerings—just as, when the ten lepers were cleansed, only the foreigner returned to give glory to God, prompting Jesus’ lament: ‘Were not ten made clean? Where are the nine?’ Even regarding the Passover, if a Gentile proselyte insists on observing it, Paul would say: though God once commanded its observance with circumcision, that requirement no longer stands, for the substance has been fulfilled in Christ; to insist on the outward rite now is to burden consciences with what was never meant to be eternal. Then comes the question: What advantage has the Jew? What profit is there in circumcision? Great in every respect. First, they were entrusted with the very oracles of God. Yet this privilege does not consist in mere possession of scrolls or mechanical recitation, but in perceiving the divine mind within them—the mysteries hidden beneath the surface. As sound reason teaches, the one who muses on divine things from personal inclination, and yet speaks of them with learned lips, is like Moses and the prophets: Jews who grasped the oracles not as texts but as truth. And if any among them resembled this, so too did the apostles of Christ, who inherited this Jewish advantage and passed it on to those who learned Christianity from them. But there is also a superior advantage for the Gentiles: from them the kingdom of God has arisen, destined to be given to a nation that bears its fruits. And if the Jews were first entrusted with the oracles, then they are also the first to have believed—for the divine deposit precedes human response, and faith follows the gift.

title: The Universality of Sin and the Faithfulness of God
english: First, we must ask: who or what comes initially? Then, who was entrusted next to perceive? It is through the one whom the Spirit grants the word of the serpent and what follows. But if someone mistakenly believes that God’s oracles are merely God’s writings, let them listen to the speaker of the psalm: the Lord’s oracles are pure words, like silver refined in fire, tested on earth, purified sevenfold. I do not think these pure words are the same as the killing letter. Just as the Jews previously mentioned were first entrusted with God’s oracles, so also some disbelieved; yet this unbelief—whether toward God or his oracles—does not annul God’s faithfulness. What then is God’s faithfulness? Is it God believing in some concerning the oracles? Or is it those entrusted with the oracles believing in God, as Abraham believed in God and it was counted to him as righteousness? I think both views have merit; for we must remember both the one who believes in God and the one entrusted with his oracles, especially in the time when scoffers mock believers, so that God’s faithfulness may not be nullified by the words of unbelievers. Let God be true though every human is a liar, as it is written, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when judged. Therefore, let it be said not as a wish, but as a declaration: may your name be blessed to the ages. What then? Shall we excel? Not at all; for we have charged both Jews and Greeks with being under sin, as it is written: there is none righteous, not even one; none who understands; none who seeks God; all have turned aside, together become worthless; none who does kindness, not even one; their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they practice deceit; the venom of asps lies under their lips; whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery lie in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known; there is no fear of God before their eyes. He desires to gather explicitly how both Jews and Greeks have come under sin, beginning from what is written: there is none righteous, not even one; none who understands; none who seeks God. We have not found these exact words elsewhere, but we believe they are drawn from the thirteenth and twenty-fifth psalms, altered by the apostle: in the eighteenth psalm, it says the Lord looked down from heaven on the children of men to see if any understand or seek God; and in the twenty-fifth, God looked down from heaven on the children of men to see if any understand or seek God. It seems they equated the act of seeing whether any understand or seek God with the declaration that none understands, none seeks God. I believe the notion of ‘none righteous, not even one’ arises from ‘none does kindness, not even one,’ and thus has been established doubly: once by alteration, once by using identical words while omitting the second mention of ‘there is none.’ The ‘venom of asps under their lips’ appears in the 138th psalm; the ‘mouth full of cursing and bitterness’ seems derived from the ninth psalm: ‘his mouth is full of cursing and bitterness and deceit.’ Next: ‘their feet are swift to shed blood’—this you will find in Isaiah or other editions of Proverbs, in the passage about the hasty to shed blood, which was marked with asterisks in the Septuagint edition. As for ‘destruction and misery in their ways,’ I have not yet located it, but I suspect it is in one of the prophets; likewise, ‘the way of peace they have not known’ I place in the prophets, and in the psalms, ‘there is no fear of God before their eyes.’ Given the multiplicity of sins, not each person is guilty of all, but some by one sin, others by another, and thus all by all. We know that whatever the law says to those under it speaks, so that every mouth may be silenced and all the world held accountable to God; for no flesh will be justified before Him by works of law, since through the law comes knowledge of sin. What is common to all flesh in the works of Moses’ law? And how does knowledge of sin come through Moses’ law, even among many who knew their own sins before Moses? title: The Revelation of God's Righteousness Apart from the Law
english: He remarks on these matters regarding our brother and what follows. Even if Job lived before Moses, he insists that even if he sinned deliberately, he concealed his transgression and what follows. Thus it seems to me that it is not the Mosaic law now being addressed to the apostle, but the natural law, which also stands written in the hearts of humanity. Who then are those under the law? Or is every person who fulfills the word a human being? For those still living apart from the law are not under it—such as Paul once was. Yet the saints whom he foreknew and predestined, he also called, justified, and glorified, both within and beyond the law; therefore their mouths will not be silenced, nor will they become guilty before God, for they are not flesh. And if they are justified, it is not by works of law, since the law does not justify through works, but through inherent righteousness. Thus, through the law comes the awareness of sin, just as through medical insight comes the recognition of illness, especially the hidden ailment and the sufferer himself. Moreover, just as the adulterer and murderer ought to be punished by law, the Lord has withdrawn the prohibition, so that it is no longer the law’s will but the grace of the lawgiver. Therefore, having spoken precisely that works of the law do not justify, he did not add 'Every person' but 'Every flesh'. For justification by intention is possible when the intention inclines toward the law, but not by works; for the works of the flesh are whatever the soul chooses. Now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, witnessed by the law and the prophets; the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all and upon all who believe. What he says is this: just as knowledge of sin does not come through the law, so neither does the revelation of God’s righteousness come through the law; for apart from the law, God’s righteousness has been revealed, surpassing natural principles, which are insufficient to grasp righteousness—not merely, but his righteousness, whose judgments are unsearchable. Therefore, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, whose teacher is Christ, receiving nothing from nature into the representation of divine righteousness. This was testified, just as by prophetic words spoken in the Holy Spirit enigmatically, and by the law of Moses the prophet. And do not wonder if two meanings of the one word 'law' are taken in the same place; for we will find this custom also in other writings; for example, do you not still say 'four-month' and 'the summer comes'? Lift up your eyes and see the land, that it is white already for summer. For twice there the harvest is named: according to the former, it refers to the bodily; according to the latter, to the spiritual. If indeed the same law is received by some, yet if apart from the law it is revealed, it is not witnessed by the law; if it is witnessed by the law, then it is not revealed apart from the law. There is no distinction; for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood. It is right to set forth those who have come after blood, according to the law of propitiations, that they may be found among the things set forth and of which the written things are symbols. It is written therefore after the sacrifice of the high priest in Leviticus, that if the whole congregation sins in ignorance, and a word escapes from the eyes of the congregation, and they do any one of the commandments of the Lord which ought not to be done, and they become guilty, and they know their sin which they have committed therein, then the congregation shall bring a young bull for the sin, and after a little while, if the priest, the anointed one, takes the blood of the bull and brings it to the tent of meeting, and again after a little while and does thus concerning the bull for the sin, so it shall be done for him and the priest shall make atonement for them and they shall be forgiven. Where then is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? By works? No, but by the law of faith. Since all boasting from works has been excluded from all people, therefore everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, even if he speaks truthfully, saying 'God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men', and what follows. But by the law of faith, all boasting is excluded which people would make who do not understand justification from faith.

Furthermore, the divine righteousness manifested apart from the law is not a mere echo of natural order but a surpassing reality, disclosed not through legal observance but through the faithful witness of Christ, who embodies it without deriving it from created principles. This revelation, attested both by the Spirit-inspired prophets and the Mosaic testament, carries a dual significance in the term 'law'—sometimes pointing to ceremonial observance, sometimes to the eternal moral order—just as we speak of 'four-month' harvests and the coming of summer, where one refers to the grain’s cycle and the other to the season’s turn. The land lies white for reaping, already ready for the sickle, symbolizing how the same divine action can be understood in bodily and spiritual senses. Those who receive the law yet find its truth revealed apart from it do not contradict the law’s witness; rather, the law points beyond itself to the grace it cannot give. All have fallen short of divine glory, yet all are justified not by merit but by the free gift of grace in Christ Jesus, the atoning sacrifice whose blood satisfies divine justice. Those who come after this sacrifice are to be received as living symbols of the true atonement, as prescribed in Leviticus: when the congregation sins unwittingly, and a command is broken unknowingly, and guilt follows awareness, they offer a bull, whose blood the priest brings into the sanctuary, making atonement and securing pardon. Thus boasting is silenced—not by human achievement, but by the law of faith, which excludes all pride rooted in works. Even the one who thanks God he is not like others shall be humbled, for true faith knows no ground for self-exaltation. And so, through faith alone, the boastful mouth is closed, and the humble heart is lifted.

title: Justification by Faith Alone: The Cross as Sole Ground of Boasting and the Law Upheld, Not Nullified
english: Boasting in legal observance has no place; Paul declares, 'Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world.' He affirms that he will glory in nothing else. Thus we conclude that a person is justified by faith, independent of works of the law. The law of faith is sufficient for justification, even for those who have done nothing. We demonstrate this through the thief on the cross and the woman who anointed Jesus’ feet with perfume, whose sins were forgiven not by deeds but by faith, and to whom he said, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace' [[Romans >> Bible:Romans 3:28]]. After coming to know the truth, sin destroys grace, as Paul will later make clear. He also maintains that even works done before faith, if they appear commendable, do not justify unless grounded in faith. Is God the God of Jews alone? Certainly not; he is also God of the Gentiles, since there is one God who justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. What advantage then does the circumcised person justified by faith have over the uncircumcised justified through faith? Not that Paul exercised his privileges differently. Just as a wife says she comes from her husband and the husband says he comes through his wife—she originates from him first, not through him; he originates from his ancestors first, then through her—so circumcision holds a position of priority, and the uncircumcised seeks justification through faith to be justified, not having originated from faith; but the believer approaches circumcision, especially the hidden kind Paul refers to, making justification by faith superior to justification through faith, just as being from a man is preferable to being through a woman. Regarding the Savior, it is not said that he came through a woman, for although all people come through women after coming from men, the Savior did not come from a man, so he came from a woman but not through her. Do we then abolish the law by faith? Certainly not! We uphold the law. Why did he say 'through faith' rather than 'by faith'? The one justified by faith is circumcision; if the law were annulled by faith, then circumcision justified by faith would be annulled; but the uncircumcised justified through faith would annul the law. Yet we received the Mosaic law through faith, not annulled, for faith establishes the law as originating from God. This is evident when speaking of genuine faith. If someone objects from 2 Corinthians about the ministry of death inscribed in stone being glorious, so that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its radiance, we ask: Is it that the law is annulled, or that we annul the law? Paul does not annul the law; if it is annulled, it is by the surpassing glory of Christ, of whom it is said he is Lord of the Sabbath, and the fading glory was not glorified in comparison to the surpassing glory. The enduring he named Christ’s; the fading, the law annulled, since the law serves as a guardian until the fullness of time. If Abraham had been justified by works, he would have had something to boast about—but not before God. For what does the Scripture say? He believed, and it was credited to him as righteousness [[Romans >> Bible:Romans 4:3]].

title: Faith Credited as Righteousness Apart from Works
english: Abraham placed his trust in God, and that trust was counted as righteousness. The text does not specify exactly what he believed about God, though the apostle seems to treat it as a general conviction. If belief were truly universal, then it would necessarily include every particular; but if Abraham only believed God concerning the specific promises made to him, it does not follow that his belief was all-encompassing, for there are degrees and measures in how one trusts God. Thus, while Abraham’s faith was credited to him as righteousness, no such reckoning is recorded when Israel witnessed the mighty acts of the Lord against Egypt, feared the Lord, and believed in Him and in Moses His servant. I suspect those from the nations who have not been careful in reading Scripture will now be presented with the explicit statement from Genesis—not as Paul placed it at the outset—but only as a bare acknowledgment that Abraham believed in God. Such a precise writer would not have framed Abraham’s belief and its reward as righteousness unless he meant to emphasize the gift nature of that credit. It is therefore likely that in the Epistle to the Romans, the apostle intends to show that it was faith—specifically Abraham’s faith—that was credited to him for righteousness. Now we turn to Abraham himself. To the one who labors, the wage is not regarded as a gift but as a debt owed; but to the one who does not work, yet trusts in the One who justifies the ungodly, that faith is counted as righteousness. Nothing that God gives to human nature as due is actually given as an obligation; rather, all is bestowed as grace. Even the good deeds performed are not done out of a sense of owed beneficence, but flow from God’s will to extend grace to whomever He chooses to bless. We must grasp this simply and universally: it applies clearly to those who work for wages and receive them not as grace but as what is due. This too can be said of those like Cain, who till the soil and do evil works—for I regard such actions as owed, as wages to be paid to sinners. Hence the apostle declares that the wages of sin are death, but no longer are the wages of God seen as owed things like eternal life; instead, eternal life is given as His grace. For He says that the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. We must not suppose that in the gospel, the principle by which you measure will be measured back to you refers to excellent works; for we stand by grace, and this is not from us, but the gift of God, so that no one may boast. Regarding the measure of our sins, the punishments must be understood as given to us.

Furthermore, just as David speaks of the blessedness of the one to whom God credits righteousness apart from works—blessed are those whose lawlessness is forgiven, whose sins are covered, blessed is the one against whom the Lord will not count sin—this blessedness, then, is it tied to circumcision or to uncircumcision? We say that Abraham’s faith was credited to him as righteousness—but how? Was it while he was circumcised, or while he was uncircumcised? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision; and he received the sign of circumcision as a seal, a seal of the righteousness that comes by faith in the uncircumcised state, so that he might be the father of all who believe without circumcision, and that righteousness might be credited to them as well. And he is father not only of the circumcised, but also of those who walk in the steps of the faith that our father Abraham had while still uncircumcised. He receives, after being justified by faith, the sign of circumcision as it were a seal.

title: Faith as the True Seal and Inheritance Beyond Law
english: When the faithful turn aside like the sealed, the mystery of those justified by faith unfolds. Those who, after believing, emerge from Abraham’s circumcision—yet remain distinct from the faithful—may be counted as his children or reckoned as his offspring, forming a people apart from the uncircumcised justified by faith. The seal remained intact as long as no one from faith and uncircumcision had arrived. But when the foretold people formed from the uncircumcised justified by faith appeared, the seal and its sign were loosed, so that it could be said to the one desiring that seal: if you circumcise, Christ profits you nothing. For the law brings wrath; where there is no law, there is no transgression. Therefore, the promise comes through faith, so that it may rest upon grace, ensuring the promise is sure for all Abraham’s seed—not only those under the law, but also those who share Abraham’s faith, who is father of us all, as it is written: ‘I have made you a father of many nations.’ Before him, he believed in God, who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not exist. One must hear the apostle here without contention and grasp his intent. Some claim: ‘If there is no law nor transgression in that place, then surely no one transgressed before Moses.’ But if no one transgressed, then no one is blameworthy—not Cain, nor those who perished in the flood due to their own sins, nor the Sodomites in transgression, nor even Adam and Eve. Yet it must be told them: the Mosaic law does not work wrath in judgment, but wrath according to itself—making some stonecutters, others burning in fire, or subjecting others to another punishment. Even where there is no law nor transgression, the law still speaks to those under the law. Observe them and the law beside Paul, called the law of faith, which works God’s wrath, and where transgression occurs when the law of faith and the law of God intersect. But clearly, he is another law—namely, the law of God, by which alone he delights in the inward man. Yet another law exists: the law in his members, warring against the law of the mind. Beware lest this be the true worker of wrath; and where there is no law, this is neither transgression. Those under this law are in no way heirs, for if those under the law are heirs, faith is rendered void. In the catalogue of charismata distributed according to the measure of faith, faith itself is enumerated—for Paul says, with other gifts, to another faith in the same Spirit. And elsewhere he declares that from God he has graciously granted you not only to attain Christ, but also to suffer for his sake. But I think the apostles, being weakly persuaded, are to be in the faith that dwells in us… Even if the heirs and the promise are to be according to grace, yet this faith which precedes grace—by which it is said that it is of faith that it might be according to grace—cannot subsist without grace. (Of the same) It is necessary, he says, it appears, to examine how being according to faith and according to grace follows the promise being sure; for if it were of the law, obtaining the sure promise would be impossible. Therefore, consider, as if a dyer were dyeing: the dyeing is made by faith concerning the soul, and especially the reasoning accounted to righteousness, so that the promise and grace through it might possess, by its inexhaustibility or immutability, certainty—which does not appear concerning the works of the law. Sometimes he feeds the righteous from his own righteousness and does evil; but I do not know whether it is written concerning faith that anyone has turned away from faith, having once been testified to have believed and been justified by faith. Then also the divine apostle seals with his testimony the thing said to him. (Of the same) [But what he says this is: as God is not a partial God but the Father of all, so also he; and again, as God is Father not according to natural kinship but according to the familiarity of faith, so also he; for obedience makes a father of all of us. title: Faith's Paradox: God's Power in Human Weakness
english: They regarded their kinship as having grasped the stronger one, thus exhibiting lordship over the word of God and lifting it upward. Following this, he demonstrates that he received this as a reward of faith; therefore, if this were not true, even if he were father of all who dwell on earth, the opposite would have no room—since the opposite is identical in nature. This is the paradox: those he did not possess by nature, he received as God’s gift. Such, he says, were the many nations whom the God who gives promises to him appointed as father. Regarding those made dead through sin, whose soul has become dead within a living body, I now believe he says: the sinner’s own soul will die. But what of those who are not, or those deprived of being and not sharing in it—thus called in opposition to those who partake in the one who said, ‘I am he who is’? He calls those who are not, so that, by obeying them, he may grant them the gift of being. title: The Once-for-All Death to Sin and Life in Christ
english: He endured death to sin in a single, definitive act; and he, having died to sin, now lives in communion with Christ. Indeed, the one who walks in newness of life walks with Christ. For the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who was given to us. This occurred precisely when we were still powerless: Christ died at the appointed moment for the ungodly. It is rare for someone to lay down their life for a righteous person—perhaps only for a genuinely good person might one find the courage to die. Yet God reveals his own love toward us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Consequently, since we have now been justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him from the wrath of God. When the text speaks of the weak or sinners, it names them and draws them into communion; but when it refers to the ungodly, it does not name them. Perhaps this distinction reflects the condition of those who live under the law: they strive by their own strength, and thus remain weak and sinful, yet they are not labeled 'ungodly' in the ordinary scriptural sense—because those under the law who transgress against God are called sinners, not ungodly. The truly ungodly are those who, though they claim to live under the law and possess its knowledge, have abandoned the God of their ancestors and turned to the gods of the nations. Before we turned to God in reverence, love had not taken root within us, for we all loved something more than God. But in that very condition—while we were still such—Christ died for us, and only then was the love of God established and made firm within us, after every obstacle to its presence had been removed by the death of Jesus. From this we must therefore listen to the ongoing establishment and confirmation of God’s love within us, a love that belongs properly to none other than God himself. As we do not merely await immortal life, but even now, as those who have become acquainted with God, are exalted in our contemplation of the Lord Christ—who, having become our mediator, brought about peace—we are called to this awareness. Therefore, if we have truly been united with him in the likeness of his death, we shall most certainly also be united with him in the likeness of his resurrection. He planted a name, having come to know a certain plant—namely, the death of Jesus—which bears fruit that destroys sin. To this plant, the word tills among those who have received instruction through Christ, making them one with him in the likeness of his death. While human nature can assume a certain likeness of that death, it cannot take on his actual death, lest it fall into sin or even come to know sin. But having died—not to cleanse sin in himself, but to cleanse sin in us—no one who has sinned can die in that same way. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, yet are justified freely, and the rest follows. In other passages, he says: God raised him up and seated him with himself in the heavenly realms in Christ; and if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above. How, then, does he say here that we too shall be in the resurrection? Let it be understood that the apostle speaks of the resurrection in two ways: first, the resurrection in which the holy one has already risen with Christ and, having risen with him, now seeks the things above; second, the resurrection that will occur when the perfect comes—of which Daniel the prophet prophesied, saying that many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Thus, the saints affirm concerning the first resurrection that they have already risen with Christ; but concerning the second, they declare that they shall rise again. If we have died with Christ, we believe we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer holds dominion over him. For what he died to, he died to sin once for all; and what he lives for, he lives to God. So too, you should regard yourselves as truly dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. He boldly affirms that death no longer rules over him—an idea that seems disgraceful to many, who claim he did not die to escape death’s rule, but willingly surrendered his soul for his sheep, or for his friends. For the Savior himself declares: No one takes my life from me; I lay it down of my own accord. Then someone might object, saying that death is now called the middle and indifferent state, as the common saying goes, that he died at that time, just as Paul says he died according to the Scriptures. But how can this be reconciled with the narrative that we died with Christ, and that what he died for, he died to sin once for all?

title: The Dual Meaning of Scripture in Bodily and Spiritual Contexts
english: It might be objected that Scripture employs identical terms in dual senses—sometimes referring to physical realities, at other times to spiritual truths—just as the encounter with the Samaritan woman presents water and drinking in the same setting, now signifying bodily thirst, now the soul’s longing. Likewise, when heat is mentioned, the reference shifts according to context. Thus, it should not surprise us that the apostle declares we have died with Christ, not to the ordinary death shared by all, but to a death from which his dominion no longer extends—a death now termed the ‘middle’ death. Another interpreter may argue that the death in view here is the sovereign death that Christ overcame, none other than his adversary, whose foreshadowing appears in the great sea creature prophesied against Jonah and lamented by Job, which he nonetheless curses—the one destined to be seized by the hand of the coming deliverer. Moving toward that death in accordance with the season of the middle death, he spoke not because of that intermediate state, but because of the ultimate one: now my soul is shaken and deeply distressed, my soul drawing near to death. For as if entering his realm through those under his control, perhaps it was for this reason declared, ‘I brought you up from the dust of death.’ And he subjected himself to him, becoming obedient even unto death. Having been condemned in him, he condemned the sin residing in that death—just as a free person might enslave himself to the enemy commander, so that, by gaining access, he could liberate his people’s economic bondage from the threat posed by that foe, through ambush slaying the commander and his forces. For the one who acts thus is not regarded as a captive taken, but as one who employs wisdom with excellence. So too Christ gave himself into servitude, that none of his disciples, instructed by the word, might become enslaved to death. As Scripture affirms, he abolished the one who held the power of death, namely the devil, and what follows. Perhaps he also surrendered himself to death, about to be dominated, flowing to rescue those under his sway, and instead offering himself over, that afterward he might assume command and abolish death. [[Romans 6:12-14 >> Bible:Romans 6:12-14]]: Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body so as to obey its desires, nor offer your members as instruments of wickedness to sin; but present yourselves to God as those raised from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God. For sin will not have dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace. Earlier he said that just as sin once reigned in death, now he does not repeat that, but says, ‘Let sin not reign in your mortal body,’ teaching that just as a throne and kingdom belong to sin, so our mortal body is its domain. For the mind set on the flesh is hostility toward God, and again, the mind set on the flesh is death. Moreover, all sins are works of the flesh, which the apostle has explicitly named. Among them, he has enumerated and taught the choices, that these too are works of the flesh, to free us from distraction, so that we do not imagine some things are works of the flesh while others are sins not of the flesh but either of soul or mind. But if anyone inquires how these choices belong among the works of the flesh, let it be said that they arise from the mind of the flesh, concerning which Paul states somewhere that he enters empty and is inflated under the mind of his flesh, yet does not lift up his head. And perhaps, when we sin while sin reigns in our mortal body, we are nothing other than that mortal body and flesh; for he does not say that my spirit remains in these people into the age because they are flesh. And this soul indeed seems not to endure, but either to become flesh through wickedness or spirit through virtue. For when it unites with the prostitute, it becomes flesh—a single entity.

title: The Believer's Identity: Dead to Sin, Alive to God in Christ
english: Think of yourselves as having died to sin, yet made alive to God through Christ Jesus. Some may interpret this as referring to those who lived for God apart from Christ Jesus. But we suggest it might not be possible to truly live for God in Christ Jesus, since even Abraham saw Christ’s day and rejoiced. If Moses served God, he did so in communion with Christ, valuing the disgrace of Christ above Egypt’s treasures. Likewise, many prophets and righteous ones longed to witness what the apostles saw and heard, yet never attained that longing, missing the life in Christ Jesus before God. You may wonder whether all who live for God in Christ Jesus must be dead to sin. One response: if someone once lived under sin, or if one enlightened by the Spirit exploring God’s depths finds those who never lived under sin yet live for God in Christ Jesus, then it appears that whoever lives for God in Christ Jesus is already dead to sin. But if all sinned because Christ died for all, then it is clear that all who live in Christ Jesus once lived under sin and later became dead to it, thus living for God in Christ Jesus. Another might argue that some are enabled to live for God in Christ Jesus without ever having been in sin, yet they are still dead to sin, just as sin was powerless before the law, not arising from prior transgression. Yet the divine apostle affirms elsewhere the ease of victory: sin will not rule over you, for you are not under law but under grace. Consider the apostolic precision: how does ruling apply? To Christ he said death no longer rules; to us he said sin will not rule—nor would it be fitting to say of Christ that sin does not rule, nor of us that death does not rule, lest the same be said of Christ and us as similar. After this, as giving cause that our sin does not rule, he says: you are not under law but under grace. For according to Paul, the power of sin is the law, and the law came in so that trespass might increase, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. Now we are under grace, not under law. For a righteous law does not lie in needing the letter’s instruction to keep God’s commandments, being taught by God, as Paul teaches concerning love: you need not write to one another, for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another. If anyone has grown together with God’s law so as not to wish the law otherwise than to be the human will, such a one is not under law but under grace. Thus we ought to think: in the Lord’s law was his will. Just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to holiness. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness. And since, as many have said (he says), we have kept watch, the name of righteousness is sometimes put in place of virtue; thus we say that now also this is what is said when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to virtue. And following the genitive of sin, the genitive of virtue is to be named righteousness in these things. Moreover, it will seem specifically that speaking of sanctification urges toward purity and bodily chastity for the one capable of receiving it. What fruit did you have then in the things you now are ashamed of? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit unto holiness, and the end is eternal life. By despising the fruit of slaves of sin as worthless talk, he says: for whatever someone formerly did in sin and ignorance, later coming to feel shame for the things committed, such fruit would be useless, unripe for food, and of no use. For the end of such works is nothing else but death, the enemy of Christ.

Thus we must understand: the law of the Lord embodies his will. Once you offered your bodily members as servants to uncleanness and lawlessness, leading only to greater lawlessness; now offer them as servants to righteousness, leading to sanctification. When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness. And since, as he notes, we have kept vigil, the term ‘righteousness’ is sometimes substituted for ‘virtue’; therefore, we say that even now, this is what is meant when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to virtue. Following the genitive of sin, the genitive of virtue is to be called righteousness in these contexts. Furthermore, it will clearly appear that speaking of sanctification calls for purity and moral integrity of life in those who are able to receive it. What gain did you reap then from the actions you now blush to recall? For the outcome of those actions is death. But now, having been liberated from sin and made servants of God, you possess the fruit that leads to holiness, and the final result is eternal life. By treating the fruit of sin’s slaves as meaningless chatter, he declares: whatever anyone once did in sin and ignorance, and later came to feel shame for those deeds, that fruit would be useless, unfit for consumption, and serving no purpose. For the end of such deeds is nothing other than death, the adversary of Christ.

title: Wages of sin, gift of life; letter-husband and Spirit's newness
english: He who said [[I am the life >> Bible:John 11:25]] rules those who have borne such fruits. In that death no one remembers God: whoever has died in it has died to God and lives to death—the same as living to sin.

Our fruit runs toward sanctification; the fruit that shames the one already aware of it is neither ours nor of our nature. That the better belongs to us and the worse does not, the Savior shows: if you were entrusted with what is alien and proved unworthy, what of your own will he give you? Even when we fail to become worthy of the better, sin keeps us from receiving it as ours by nature.

Some say the sanctifying fruit of those enslaved to God is complete purity from sexual pleasure. On that reading, [[having been freed from sin you became slaves of righteousness >> Bible:Romans 6:18]] fits those in marriage, while the stronger word [[but now that you have been freed from sin >> Bible:Romans 6:22]] fits those in chastity. So the person whose final fruit is sanctification through slavery to God was already enslaved to righteousness earlier, yet may still lack that sanctifying fruit because of the word spoken by way of concession.

[[For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord >> Bible:Romans 6:23]]. The contrast is deliberate: wages for sin, gift for God. God does not pay wages as a debt; he gives a gift. Sin does not give a gift; it pays what is owed. Nor does he simply call the gift 'eternal life,' for that life is incomplete when it is not in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Sin deals death to the one it rules; God does not bring Christ's enemy, death—[[God did not make death >> Bible:Wisdom 1:13]]. If someone answers with [[I kill and I make alive >> Bible:Deuteronomy 32:39]] and [[the Lord kills and makes alive >> Bible:1 Samuel 2:6]], we say God kills sin so that afterward he may make alive the one who has died to sin.

[[Or do you not know, brothers—for I speak to those who know the law—that the law rules a person as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her living husband; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law of the husband. So while the husband lives she will be called an adulteress if she belongs to another; but if the husband dies she is free from the law and is not an adulteress if she belongs to another >> Bible:Romans 7:1-3]].

To know the law fully is to know the difference inside it between the oldness of the letter and the newness of the spirit in its meanings. That is perfect knowledge of the law. His example fits tightly: the married woman is bound to the living husband; if he dies she is released. The husband is the law—clearly the letter-law—which can die because it is the oldness of the letter; what grows old and ages nears disappearance. It is even said to die when it no longer truly lives among those who still claim to keep it.

[[But now we have been released from the law, having died to that which held us, so that we serve in newness of spirit and not in oldness of letter >> Bible:Romans 7:6]]. The Holy Spirit is always new—neither aging nor wearing out—while our inner self is renewed day by day. The oldness of the letter was never new, and our old self was never young: it aged at once, not by the clock but by the thoughts and deeds that made it old.

[[What then? Is the law sin? >> Bible:Romans 7:7]] 'Law' is one word, but Scripture does not mean one thing by it everywhere. At each place you must ask what 'law' signifies now. The same holds for many other shared names in Scripture that confuse readers who think one sound means one sense wherever it appears. Leaving aside harder cases that need construction and replies, it is enough to shame anyone into admitting that 'law' is laid on several realities.

title: The Twofold Meaning of Law: Letter and Spirit
english: For instance, when the Epistle to the Galatians declares that those who rely on works of the law stand under a curse, quoting Scripture: 'Cursed is everyone who fails to uphold every command written in the book of the law,' it becomes evident that the law as given by Moses comprises both prescriptive demands—what must be done—and prohibitive warnings—what must be avoided—by those subject to it. This dual character is reinforced elsewhere in the same letter, where we learn the law was added due to transgressions, serving as a temporary guardian until the promised offspring arrived, instituted through angelic mediation. Likewise, the law functioned as our custodian until Christ, so that justification might come through faith; but once faith emerged, we are no longer under such supervision, for all who believe in Christ Jesus are sons of God. The historical narrative authored by Moses is thus revealed as an expression of the law’s voice, as when the Galatian epistle challenges: 'Tell me, you who wish to be under the law, do you not hear what it says?' For it is recorded that Abraham had two sons—one by the slave woman, born according to the flesh, and one by the free woman, born through promise. I also recognize the Psalms as bearing the name 'law,' since their fulfillment is seen in the words: 'I ate them with gladness.' Furthermore, the prophecy of Isaiah is termed 'law' by the apostle, citing: 'It is written in the law: I will speak to this people with strangers’ tongues and foreign lips; yet even then they will not listen,' declares the Lord—a sentiment I find echoed in Aquila’s translation. Moreover, the law is understood not only in its external form but also in its deeper, spiritual dimension, as we affirm: 'The law is spiritual.' Beyond this, the law is described as that which is inwardly implanted by common notions and, as Scripture affirms, 'written on the heart'—a word that prescribes duty and forbids transgression. This is further confirmed when Gentiles, who lack the law by nature, nevertheless perform its requirements; they become a law to themselves, demonstrating the work of the law inscribed in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness, their thoughts either accusing or excusing them. For the law written in the hearts and practiced by Gentiles through nature is none other than that which is innately engraved in the rational faculty by common conception, now being more fully realized in our time. This understanding of the law was operative even before sin was imputed in the absence of law, or known only through law; for prior to the Mosaic law, sin was charged to Cain and to those in the flood, and still to the Sodomites and countless others, and many had knowledge of sin long before Moses. There is no need to be surprised when a single term like 'law' carries two meanings in the same context, for this pattern appears elsewhere—for example, when you do not say: 'Is it four-monthly, and does summer come?' Lift your eyes and behold the land: it is already white for harvest. Indeed, the harvest is named twice—first referring to the physical gathering, then to the spiritual ingathering. The same duality appears in the man born blind who was healed; when addressed in bodily terms, He declared: 'I have come into this world so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.' Thus, apart from the law of nature, God’s righteousness has been unveiled, attested by the law of Moses and the prophets. Yet to those still hesitant to accept the twofold sense of 'law,' we might say: if the same law is received both now and apart from it, and God’s righteousness is revealed in both cases, witnessed by law and prophets, then if it is revealed apart from the law, it is not witnessed by the law; if witnessed by the law, it is not separate from it. But concerning the righteousness of God revealed in Jesus Christ, the law of nature bears no testimony at all, for it is inferior to it; whereas the Mosaic law—not in its letter but in its spirit, along with those who embody its spirit—the prophets, and the indwelling spiritual word—do bear witness. Therefore, let the attentive reader of sacred Scripture observe that writings do not always employ identical terms for identical realities, yet they do so intentionally, sometimes…

title: Romans catena (u05-open)
english: At times we must interpret a word according to its plain meaning, at others figuratively, and occasionally because the context requires a different sense—either as it stands or as it appears elsewhere in Scripture. By observing this carefully, we avoid many mistakes and unfounded suppositions. Therefore, we must recognize that what has been perceived is not always located in the same reality; sometimes it is bodily sight, sometimes spiritual discernment. This principle must be universally understood: when the divine purpose is to conceal truth rather than reveal it openly to the Spirit in the prophets and to the Word of Christ in the apostles, the phrasing often becomes complex and does not follow a single, straightforward sequence. This is done so that the unworthy, upon encountering what is secretly reserved for their benefit, do not bring judgment upon themselves by seizing what was meant to remain hidden. This is frequently the reason why some suppose that Scripture as a whole lacks syntax and coherence—especially the prophetic and apostolic writings, and most notably Paul’s letter to the Romans, where legal matters are named differently and placed in varied contexts, making it seem as though Paul deviates from his stated purpose. But what shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Yet I would not have known sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness had the law not declared, 'You shall not covet.' Thus we understand the law not merely as Moses’ prohibition against covetousness, but also as the natural law ingrained in us—for desire is naturally implanted in us as a passion, and sin has seized opportunity not only through the written commandment but also through this inner law. Even Adam knew this before the Mosaic law. Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetousness—not only in me, but in every soul when sin awakens, all covetousness wages war against the human race; for it is impossible for a human soul not to fall into passions, even if later, through discipline, it appears, as it were, to attain impassibility. Paul declares that all covetousness is passionate and sinful—which the law forbids by teaching, 'You shall not covet'—and this is an irrational impulse arising from mere urge, overflowing beyond reason, by which we cling to life, desiring good, the middling and indifferent life, attaching ourselves to wealth, honor, women, and other covetous things, doing the will of sin, thus stretching ourselves toward what we imagine to be good upon all that we desire. For the fantasy of good becomes covetousness. Apart from the law, sin is powerless. I once lived apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died, and I found that the very commandment meant for life became death to me—for sin, seizing opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and thereby killed me. Then it could be said of such a person that he lives apart from the law; for upon this condition, reflecting, Paul and every person would say, I once lived apart from the law, when, as he says, on the eighth day after birth, of the race of Israel, a Hebrew of the Hebrews—for it is not possible for an irrational infant, possessing a state, to live under law. Indeed, every person has lived apart from the law at some time, namely in childhood, when there was no reproof, for ignorance is not subject to punishment; and the commandment has come at some time to every person—but when did they fulfill the word, and understand the commandment enjoining such things and forbidding such things? And at the very moment the commandment came, in its first occurrence, wickedness arose—or, as Paul called it, sin awoke, having been dead; for since it is not natural for sin and humanity to coexist, therefore, when the commandment came, sin awoke and the soul died, according to the soul, the sinner, this one shall die. title: The Law's Role in Revealing Sin and Death
english: The goodness embedded in the law, meant to guide life, paradoxically becomes a catalyst for death—since sin lacks definition apart from the law, and condemnation requires its boundary, yet it is through the law that sin’s guilt and punishment are formally established. Do not confuse the initial death of sin with its final demise; there is a profound distinction between sin lying inert without the law’s demand and sin being put to death through the Spirit’s mortification of our earthly nature; thus, the lifeless state of sin in each scenario produces vastly different outcomes in spiritual vitality, and they cannot be equated by any measure of lived experience. Indeed, sin remains deadly as long as our bodily impulses remain un subdued by the divine word, and even before the law was given, sin held sway over humanity. Yet someone might object: even if sin seizes the commandment as an occasion to deceive and destroy, we must still affirm the truth and embrace the law inscribed on the heart by God as holy, and honor the command as good, flowing from the God of goodness. So, has this good become death to me? Certainly not! But sin, in order to be exposed as sin through the very good that works death in me, so that through the commandment sin might be revealed as utterly sinful. If someone objects, saying, 'Perhaps the holy law has become death to humanity?'—know this: when the commandment arrived, sin sprang back to life and the person died—let them understand that it was not the good that turned into death, but that sin must be made manifest in its true evilness; for when the good dwells in the soul, evil is unveiled, and if one then sins, it becomes clear that the commandment, which identified evil and warned against it, serves as the occasion of death, and sin—not merely sin, but sin in its most aggravated form—enters through the holy command and brings about our destruction. We acknowledge that the law is spiritual, yet I remain fleshly, enslaved to sin. A question emerges from all this: how can Paul say these things without appearing to contradict himself when he declares we were bought with a price, Christ redeemed us, and yet I no longer live, but Christ lives in me? Unless we allow that the Word assumes different persons, and the passages are tailored to distinct personal realities, in which the foolish act contrary to their original intent. This discourse is fitting for those who have come to know the law as divine and see its commands as good, yet, as those still enslaved to sin and governed by the flesh, they do not know how to resist and thus fall into transgression. For what I do, I do not understand; for what I wish to do, I do not do, but what I detest, that I perform. These words suit those who have weakened toward passion due to feeble reasoning, and those who, at times, are overcome by anger and fear and act against their will and their deepest aversions; but when, having been defeated by intellectual pride, we are conquered by what appears good but is not true, we endorse the law in word while doing what pleases us. For I delight in God’s law according to the inner self, yet I perceive another law in my members waging war against the law of my mind and leading me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my flesh. In those who have not yet fortified themselves toward virtue, Paul outlines this present reality: just as a soldier who has taken captive enemies leads them away, so in these individuals, the law in their members opposes the law of their mind, enslaves the miserable soul, and drives it toward the law of sin residing in the bodily members. Miserable man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. As one who weakens the human frailty that drags and distracts reason and incites opposition, he cries, 'Wretched man that I am'; and as one delivered by divine aid from the body named the body of death for these very reasons, he adds, 'I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ.' title: Likeness of sinful flesh; fleshly mindset versus Spirit's help
english: [[God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, and condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit >> Bible:Romans 8:3-4]].

Here he speaks of what the law of sin and death cannot do. Virtue is strong by its own nature; vice and what comes from it are weak and powerless. Vice rules not the strong but the slack—not by its own strength but by their feebleness. Such a 'law' is powerless by nature, so it worked in weak flesh.

God condemned that law by sending his Son not in flesh of the sin that slaves of the law of sin serve, but in a likeness of such flesh. The Son's flesh was not sin but likeness, because it did not come from a man's seed and a woman joined in sleep. So God condemned sin become exceedingly sinful, and through the flesh the divine law's righteous requirement is fulfilled in us when we do not walk according to flesh—where that powerless weakness, which is vice, works—but follow God according to his Spirit and receive the Son into ourselves.

[[Because the mindset of the flesh is enmity toward God, for it is not subject to the law of God, nor can it be; and those who are in the flesh cannot please God >> Bible:Romans 8:7-8]]. From Paul we learn who walk according to flesh—those who mind fleshly things—and who according to Spirit—those who mind the Spirit's things.

Fleshly mindsets are fornication, wantonness, idolatry, and the like—death itself. The Spirit's fruit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, and what follows—life. Such people are already in life and rejoice in peace. Those who sow to the flesh reap corruption; those who live by the Spirit sow of the Spirit and reap eternal life. Those of the flesh's mindset are also God's enemies.

People who want riches or glory also mind fleshly things. Jews who live by the letter and practice visible circumcision in the flesh mind the fleshly side of the law; Jews in secret, who circumcise heart and spirit, mind the Spirit's things. In the fleshly mindset of the law you find death and enmity toward God; in the Spirit's mindset of the law, life and peace. Those in the flesh of the law cannot please God; those in the Spirit of the law can. Both profess Moses' law, yet they take it according to flesh and we according to Spirit—so they reckon the promises fleshy, while we take them as spiritual blessing in the heavenlies.

[[Hope that is seen is not hope; for what one sees, why still hope? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with endurance >> Bible:Romans 8:24-25]]. Other copies read something like 'if he is eager he endures what he sees'; but greatness belongs to the one who hopes toward what is unseen and, stretching the mind toward it, endures whatever comes.

[[Likewise the Spirit helps our weaknesses; for we do not know what we ought to pray, but the Spirit itself intercedes for us with unspoken groanings >> Bible:Romans 8:26]]. It fills up what our weakness lacks. Through this, all human nature is shown. In countless ways the Spirit helps our weakness, not least when we pray and cross over so as to pray in spirit. Not knowing what to pray as we ought, helped by the Spirit we pray in spirit; then with the mind following that help we pray with the mind too. Prayer that uses only one is incomplete, as [[if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:14]] shows. So that the mind may bear fruit, he says: I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind. [[What then… >> Bible:Romans 8:31]]…
